Here’s a New EDC Adjustable Wrench Multi-Tool for Your Collection

Oct 2, 2026 Stuart 21 Comments

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 1:20
Instaread
If you buy something through our links, ToolGuyd might earn an affiliate commission.

EDC tool fans, here’s another mini tool for your collection – a Workpro 4-inch adjustable wrench with removable pry bar.

It’s a compact wrench with 1-inch max opening width.

It comes with a multi-functional pry bar that can be removed. The pry bar is magnetically secured within the wrench handle.

Advertisement

Workpro built box end wrenches into the pry bar, in 4mm, 5mm, 6mm, 7mm, and 8mm sizes.

When attached to the wrench, a 1/4″ hex bit cutout can work with standard screwdriver bits.

It also has a notch for pulling nails, although you might not get much leverage from the diminutively sized tool, and a 0-2″ ruler.

You can buy it in black or silver finishes. There’s a slight price different between the two options.

Price: $17-$18 at the time of this posting

Buy it at Amazon

As a reminder, Amazon Prime Day is next week.

Advertisement

Discussion

I bought 4-inch adjustable wrenches before, and find them to be a bit of a novelty. This one also gives you a mini pry bar.

It’s multi-functional, but is it practical?

There are a bunch of other tiny adjustable wrenches.

Channellock’s has the smallest head I’ve seen (pro for compact storage, con for jaw capacity, I love using mine).

Crescent used to have the least expensive one I knew of (it’s affordable at just $10).

Workpro has a cheap one that looks bulky.

Workpro also has one with extra wide jaw opening.

And one with slim jaws.

  4. MM

    2 days ago

    I have a pair of 4″ Bahco adjustable wrenches, 1960’s/70’s vintage. They have smaller jaws than this Workpro, which in one way makes them a bit less useful since they can only be used on smaller fasteners. However they are also very thin and light. Throw one in your pocket and you don’t notice its there. My favorite use for them was nuts on panel-mount switches, LED holders, and so on–anything you’d mount to a control panel using those extremely thin jam nuts common on electronics. I used these quite often until I recently got a set of plastic sockets made specifically for that purpose. The advantage that these tiny adjustable wrenches have is that they can fit right up against a panel and they have no chamfer on the working edges where they engage those thin jam nuts properly. Ordinary sockets don’t work well because the chamfer on the mouth of the socket is often larger than the nut. Pliers Wrenches are great, but the pushbutton and the handles are wider than the jaws, which means they don’t fit up against a panel.

    Reply

  12. JoeM

    19 hours ago

    I’ve had to think about this before answering. Nothing serious, just going through every use I’ve ever had for a pocketable wrench, such as this one. The uses are very slim for me (no pun intended) but there is a specific use that stands out for me. One I had to deal with over a decade ago, when I did some major purchasing of Dremel products, and the attachments for them. The Workstation, Plunge Router, Glue Gun (Model 1200, best one I’ve ever used in my life, sadly discontinued long before its time.) and a few other various tools in the lineup (at the time, discontinuations have happened since.) needed an unsupplied Wrench to use as a tightening point, for various assembly nuts and bolts. The standard two flat-stamped Dremel Wrenches for the Attachment Nut, and the Collet Nut, are the wrong size for these fastening points.

    When I solved this issue, I bought a super-inexpensive (I believe they were $4 each, maybe $7? Mastercraft brand at Canadian Tire.) 4″ or 6″ adjustable wrench for all the different Dremel points that might need one. Something I could leave with the tools, and not be concerned about losing them, because I had bought several of them. Cheap, available as needed, does the job.

    Given the size of this Workpro, perhaps this wrench would work well in the same applications. I’m not sure. The price is significantly higher than my solution wrenches, but the ability to hide it away along with the tools that need one, without it taking up much space, would probably be the best use I could find for it. It is, unfortunately, significantly more expensive, so I would have to go looking for the absolute minimum number I needed, rather than buying them willy-nilly for every single place that kinda-sorta needed one. I don’t see a need for the depicted use of it, as I have Leatherman Tools for that. But a small, easily kept near to the required fasteners that get regularly adjusted by it, wrench does seem like a valid use for this. Yeah, it does a lot more than that, and the company is decent, but, it’s a little late in the game to buy it for myself. I got its roles covered rather completely by other tools by now. But it does seem like good quality.
